Far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was taken into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody on Friday, according to agency records reviewed by Newsweek, renewing attention on his yearslong ties to both President Donald Trump's MAGA movement and rapper Kanye West's political and business ventures.
The British-born activist was detained in Louisiana while in New Orleans ahead of a scheduled concert by West, according to CBS News.
Why Was Milo Yiannopoulos Arrested by ICE?
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek via email that Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on August 27 after allegedly overstaying his visa. The agency said the British national entered the United States legally through New York in May 2019 but later remained in the country unlawfully, describing him as having "chosen to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws."
DHS said an immigration judge issued Yiannopoulos a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to appear for an immigration hearing. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings, the department said.
The agency also pointed to the case as evidence of the Trump administration's tougher immigration enforcement policies. In a statement, DHS said it had ended what it called a "Biden-era policy" that allowed people in the country illegally to travel domestically by air and warned that those who do not leave voluntarily could face arrest and deportation.
Conservative political activist Laura Loomer claimed credit for Yiannopoulos' ICE detention, resharing a post from March in which she'd accused him of living in the U.S. with an expired visa. "Milo Yiannopoulos is in ICE custody after I exposed his illegal alien lifestyle," the Trump ally wrote on X.
Milo Yiannopoulos and Donald Trump Ties Explained
Yiannopoulos first became nationally known during Trump's 2016 presidential campaign as a Breitbart editor and one of the most prominent figures associated with the emerging "alt-right" movement.
Although he fell from grace in conservative circles following a 2017 controversy over remarks about relationships between adults and teenage boys, he remained a recognizable figure in Trump-world politics and among some MAGA activists for years afterward.
Milo Yiannopoulos and Kanye West Ties Explained
His most significant role in recent years came through his association with West, now known as Ye. In 2022, Yiannopoulos became involved in the rapper's political orbit as West explored a 2024 presidential run and generated controversy with a string of antisemitic remarks and other inflammatory statements.
Yiannopoulos stepped away from West's campaign in December 2022.
"Ye and I have come to the mutual conclusion that I should step away from his political team. Ye is a genius whom I have come to love and respect. We remain friends. I will continue to pray for Ye and all his endeavors," Yiannopoulos wrote on his Telegram channel Sunday.
In a separate post, which appears to have been deleted but was viewed and captured in a screenshot by Newsweek at the time, the far-right provocateur suggested he and West disagreed over staffing for the 2024 campaign.
"For the record, I had concerns about a potential new hire, but I never tried to get anyone fired—especially not people I personally brought in, who owe me their gratitude, loyalty and respect," Yiannopoulos wrote in the now-deleted post.
What Is Milo Yiannopoulos' View on Immigration?
For years, the British-born political commentator has been one of the most outspoken advocates of hard-line immigration enforcement, frequently calling for mass deportations and an expanded role for ICE.
“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos wrote on X last year.
Yiannopoulos has repeatedly argued that immigration enforcement should be a top priority for Republican administrations. In social media posts highlighted in recent reporting, he called for the deportation of "millions and millions of people," writing that "without that, nothing else matters."
He has also backed a significantly heightened enforcement presence by ICE. According to multiple reports, Yiannopoulos suggested California should have ICE checkpoints at locations including supermarkets, gas stations and government buildings, coupled with immediate deportation for people unable to prove they were legally present in the U.S. He has additionally advocated for broader protections for immigration officers carrying out enforcement actions.
The development Friday places Yiannopoulos in the unusual position of facing the same immigration enforcement system he spent years urging the government to strengthen.
Where Is Milo Yiannopoulos From?
Yiannopoulos was born in Kent, England, and is a British citizen. Before becoming a prominent figure in U.S. conservative politics, he built a career in the United Kingdom as a technology journalist and commentator. He later moved to the United States, where he gained national attention through his work at Breitbart News and his support for Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.
His profile grew rapidly during the rise of the alt-right movement, with speaking tours, media appearances and a large social media following helping make him one of the era's most recognizable conservative commentators. Milo Yiannopoulos has reportedly been detained by ICE in Louisiana, according to TMZ, which cited inmate records showing him held at an ICE detention center and sources saying he was taken into custody at an airport.

Yiannopoulos is British. He was born in England in October 1984 under the name Milo Hanrahan and later took his Greek grandmother’s surname. He is not an American citizen and never has been. In February 2017, at the press conference where he announced his resignation from Breitbart, he said he lives in the United States on an O-1 visa, the category reserved for people with extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics.
He also spent years turning immigration enforcement into a stage act. At the University of New Mexico in January 2018, he wore a police vest and displayed the ICE tip hotline number on a giant screen behind him with the instruction “Purge your local illegals.” He used the same slogan on an LED billboard at another campus appearance, with the ICE phone number printed alongside it. Ahead of his canceled 2017 event at UC Berkeley, a professor said reliable sources indicated he planned to publicly name undocumented students at the school. In 2018, he staged a photo shoot at a mock Western Wall, wearing a kippah with ICE printed on it and placing a prayer note asking for speedy deportations.The rest of the record is long and documented.
Twitter permanently banned him in July 2016 for inciting targeted abuse of Leslie Jones during the release of the “Ghostbusters” reboot. Jones, who is Black, was flooded with racist and sexist messages, including images comparing her to apes and fake tweets fabricated to look like they came from her own account. She left the platform, writing that she was in a personal hell and asking Twitter to do more. The Associated Press, Reuters, and BuzzFeed all reported that Yiannopoulos led or directed much of the campaign. Twitter’s suspension email said he was removed for repeated violations of the rules prohibiting participating in or inciting targeted abuse of individuals. He called the ban cowardly and said he was targeted for being a gay conservative. Facebook banned him in 2019.
In late 2017, BuzzFeed News published leaked emails from his time at Breitbart showing he solicited story ideas and editing suggestions from white nationalists, including Devin Saucier, an editor at American Renaissance. He resigned from Breitbart in February 2017 and lost his Simon and Schuster book deal in the same stretch, after video surfaced of him describing sexual relationships between adult men and boys as young as 13 as something that happens, in his words, perfectly consensually.In March 2019, Australia banned him from entering the country over his response to the Christchurch mosque massacre, which killed 51 people. He had written on Facebook that attacks like it happen because the establishment panders to and mollycoddles extremist leftism and what he called barbaric, alien religious cultures. Immigration Minister David Coleman said the comments were appalling and fomented hatred and division. The ban came a week after Coleman had approved his visa over the objection of the Home Affairs department, which had warned he might fail the country’s character test. Labor MP Tony Burke said the department already had enough evidence to bar him and that the tours for the world’s hate speakers had to stop.

In March 2024, there were 412 people nationwide held in immigration detention for more than a year. By March 2026, the last time ICE released detention statistics, that number had grown to 2,220. Louisiana’s federal courts have been flooded with habeas petitions from detainees arguing they are being held unlawfully, more than 1,200 in the first five months of 2026 alone, compared with 291 across the entire five years from 2020 through 2024. Nationally, ICE held 65,765 people in detention as of July 11, and roughly 70 percent of them had no criminal conviction.Whether Yiannopoulos remains in that system for any length of time, and on what basis he was taken into it, is not yet known.
